Intent: Open on the locked-room discovery: Ellis arrives at Harben House, meets Inspector Lane and Anna, and is shown the study that is locked from the inside with Lucius Harben dead. Establish stakes, the room's layout (longcase clock, display case, desk), the brass key in the lock, the torn note in the victim's hand and the initial puzzle—no gun on display.

The P0 and P1 material is already assembled and is below. You cannot change it.
Your job is what it does not know to look for: something established long ago that
this scene touches, a promise falling due, a place or object that has been described
before, a relationship whose history matters here.
Search the index with the shell, and **batch it**. One command can answer several
questions, and one reply can carry several tool calls — measured, you averaged 22.5
round-trips per build with 96% of them carrying a single read, each re-sending a
transcript that had grown to 12,000 tokens to get one file back. That loop is most of
what a run spends and most of how long it takes.
So decide what you want, then ask for it all at once. `read_index` takes a **list** of
paths — one call for ten files costs one round-trip, ten calls cost ten:
  read_index paths=["characters/char-a/profile.yaml", "objects/obj-key.yaml", …]
  grep -rn "<id-a>\|<id-b>\|<id-c>" novel/chapters/ | tail -40
  cat characters/*/state.jsonl continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl relations/<a>--<b>.yaml
  ls relations/ objects/ locations/
A second round-trip is worth it when what you read next depends on what came back. It
is not worth it for a list of files you had already chosen.

This scene is in the opening third. There is little behind it, so recall is cheap and mostly unnecessary — check the scene before it and the entity files, and do not pad. An item added here is an item the writer and the verifier both read.
Add what you find with add_context_item. Quote the material; a pointer is not context.
Add nothing if there is nothing — a padded packet costs the writer attention it needs
for the scene, and every item you add is also an item the verifier reads.
Then record what you could **not** find, with note_gap. Read the scene's intent and ask
what a writer must know to write it: what this place looks like, whether these two have
met, what exactly was promised. For each one you searched for and did not find, note it.
This half matters as much as the first. What you add, the writer uses; what you record
as missing is what the writer would otherwise invent without noticing it was inventing —
and an invented fact is indistinguishable from an established one the moment it is on
the page.

Everything you add is assembled into .context-builder/history/ch-01/s-001.md, which is the document the writer works from. If it asks a follow-up later, your answer is appended to that same file rather than sent as a loose reply — so answer as though you were adding to the packet, because you are.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

This is the opening scene. Assemble context: the study's precise floorplan around the clock, desk and display case; the state of the longcase clock (its hands, whether it is stopped and at what minute, access panel latched or removed); the foyer layout and the locked study door with the brass key in the lock; who found the body and when; the torn note's text fragment that is visible; the ivory revolver's initial status (missing from display). Provide the packet the writer will need: police presence level, mood, time of day, weather, and the household's immediate reactions. Include verbatim where relevant: the torn note's visible words, Anna's initial line when Ellis arrives, and Inspector Lane's opening instruction. Also indicate any known constraints (e.g., window latched; no forced entry).

That is in addition to the above, not instead of it.

### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Open on the locked-room discovery: Ellis arrives at Harben House, meets Inspector Lane and Anna, and is shown the study that is locked from the inside with Lucius Harben dead. Establish stakes, the room's layout (longcase clock, display case, desk), the brass key in the lock, the torn note in the victim's hand and the initial puzzle—no gun on display.
Present: char-ellis-fletcher, char-inspector-margot-lane, char-anna-rowe, char-lucius-harben, loc-harben-study, loc-harben-foyer, obj-longcase-clock, obj-brass-key, obj-torn-note, obj-ivory-revolver
Target length: about 700 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

A private detective, called to a locked study where a reclusive horologist lies shot, must pry open a case where an ornate clock, a missing antique revolver, a torn note and a quiet household hide a carefully timed murder — and the closer he gets, the more someone tries to reset the hands of time.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-ellis-fletcher: Private detective and the story's first-person narrator. Mid-forties, methodical, wry, a former police investigator who left under a cloud.
- char-lucius-harben: The victim. A reclusive horologist and collector of rare clocks and antique weapons; lived alone with a small staff at Harben House.
- char-iris-harben: Lucius's wife. Younger than her husband, composed in public, financially and emotionally entangled in his collection and reputation.
- char-thomas-reed: Lucius's former apprentice and business partner. Expert on clocks, brusque, had recent arguments with Lucius about a disputed sale.
- char-anna-rowe: Housekeeper at Harben House. Practical, observant, the person who found the body and summoned the police.
- char-inspector-margot-lane: Local police inspector assigned to the case. Respectful of Ellis but protective of procedure; cautious about letting a private eye meddle.
- loc-harben-study: Lucius Harben's private study: a compact, well-appointed room lined with books and clocks, dominated by an ornate longcase clock and a display case of antique weapons.
- loc-harben-foyer: The small foyer outside the study; the study's only door opens into this area. The rest of Harben House is silent and oak-paneled.
- obj-longcase-clock: An ornate longcase (grandfather) clock, a prized item in Lucius's collection. It has visible hands, a striking mechanism, and an access panel in its case.
- obj-ivory-revolver: A small antique single-shot revolver from Lucius's weapon display: ivory grips, gilded barrel. At the start of the case its status (in-place/missing/found) is a question to be resolved in the investigation.
- obj-brass-key: A heavy brass key used for the study's lock. It is found in the study's lock when the room is discovered locked; custody and origin matter.
- obj-torn-note: A scrap of paper found clutched in Lucius's hand with part of a sentence visible. Its provenance and whether it is genuine or planted is in question.
- obj-black-thread: A length of thin black thread (waxed linen / monofilament) found tangled behind the clock — a small, apparently insignificant physical clue that ties into mechanical timing.
- obj-envelope: A sealed envelope found on Lucius's desk containing a terse typed threat about an upcoming sale; the handwriting on the flap is later compared to suspects.

### narrative-voice  <novel/style/voice.md>

Narration: first person, char-ellis-fletcher, past tense. This was decided for the whole book before any of it was written and does not change.
Check your own sentences against it before you stage them. Mixing a collective "we" into a third-person narration, or slipping into present tense for a scene that feels immediate, is scored as a defect and is the most common one this system has produced: seven of nine consistency errors in a measured 18,000-word manuscript were exactly this.
If you think the story genuinely needs a different voice, propose the deviation — do not simply write it.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural elements or 'impossible' physics — every action must be explainable by real mechanisms or human trickery.
- The narrator, Ellis, cannot know anything he didn't observe, be told, or reasonably infer; revelations must come by evidence or deduction shown in-scene.
- Forensic details (gunshot residue, fingerprints, time of death signs) must be internally consistent and not contradicted later.
- All significant objects, locations and characters used in scenes must be declared as entities above; later scenes may only refer to these ids.
- Locked-room constraints are physical: doors and windows can only be manipulated by plausible mechanical means or realistic sleight, and any trick must be demonstrable within the story's scenes.
- No retroactive retcons of committed facts; if a gap exists it must be acknowledged as such in the prose and can be left unresolved.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

### novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md
The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

I went back into the study with Lane’s caution still hanging between us. She closed the door behind her and said, in the very words she’d used when I first arrived, “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” The sentence landed like a rule; her eyes supplied everything she didn’t say.

The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

I went back into the study with Lane’s caution still hanging between us. She closed the door behind her and said, in the very words she’d used when I first arrived, “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” The sentence landed like a rule; her eyes supplied everything she didn’t say.

The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural elements or 'impossible' physics — every action must be explainable by real mechanisms or human trickery.
- The narrator, Ellis, cannot know anything he didn't observe, be told, or reasonably infer; revelations must come by evidence or deduction shown in-scene.
- Forensic details (gunshot residue, fingerprints, time of death signs) must be internally consistent and not contradicted later.
- All significant objects, locations and characters used in scenes must be declared as entities above; later scenes may only refer to these ids.
- Locked-room constraints are physical: doors and windows can only be manipulated by plausible mechanical means or realistic sleight, and any trick must be demonstrable within the story's scenes.
- No retroactive retcons of committed facts; if a gap exists it must be acknowledged as such in the prose and can be left unresolved.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-003.md>

I went back into the study with Lane's warning folded into the hollow of a sentence I couldn't spend. She'd told me not to touch anything until forensics arrived; I left my hands in my coat and let my eyes do the work. The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. The access panel at the back was a hair ajar; the brass inside looked thumbed, varnish rubbed away where skin or a tool had rested. Fine, fresh scores ringed the latch—hairline marks that flashed when the light caught them, as if a slender implement had been used to lever it.

At the base the black thread hung where I'd seen it: waxed, stiff, snagged on a screw. I followed its line: it looped and ran up toward the movement and vanished behind the plates. That was no stray sewing fibre; laid like that it could be a patient little mechanism, a thing that might nudge a wheel at an appointed minute.

Thomas Reed came in from the workshop, bringing the faint smell of oil with him. He had the thumb-and-forefinger rub that tells you a man is working through a thought. "You were in here recently?" I asked.

He met my gaze. "I was in three days ago to wind it and I stripped the weight-gear to clean the pivots—it's delicate work, Ellis." He paused, then added, "I was out of the shop just before eleven. Ask anyone." The admission sat in the room like a small brass cog: useful, precise, and easily checked.

"You left the panel closed?" I said.

"I always close it when I'm done," he said. He rubbed his thumb as if to work a stubborn splinter free. "I didn't kill him, if that's what you're getting at. I serviced it—winding, cleaning the pivots—but I was gone by then." His voice tightened on the last word.

Lucius's fingers curled around a torn scrap. The ragged edge lay on top of the knuckles; the torn fibres splayed against the skin rather than pressed into it. The blotter beneath showed a neat, round stain—the dark halo of a single shot. The scrap sat on that halo without a smear. If he'd clutched the paper in his last moments the fibres would have been pressed, ink and blood rubbed into the edge. This looked arranged.

"The scrap was put there after the fact," I said, careful to keep my tone even. Accusation is heavy; Lane was watching.

Thomas's face went slack. "Why would someone do that? To make it look—" He stopped.

Forensics arrived just then. They moved with the efficiency of people who practise restraint: a gloved hand to lift, a small vacuum for trace, a careful photograph. The tech at the desk tapped the envelope's diagonal crease with a latexed fingertip. "We lifted a partial print from the flap's crease," he said. "Preliminary lift consistent with Iris Harben."

Iris came in as if the name had called her. She kept her composure; the small motion of smoothing her wedding band was the private thing I'd noticed before. When I asked about the sale and the note she answered with a bluntness that might be armour. "If he sells it, we have nothing left but his arrogance."

For a moment the study felt like a display cabinet for evidence: the stopped hands at eleven-seventeen, the access panel scored with fresh marks, the black thread threading toward the gears, a torn note that read like stagecraft, and an envelope that now carried a lifted print. I kept my hands where Lane could see them and stepped to the clock's case without touching the latch. Forensics had the gloves and the reasons.

What I thought, and was careful not to say out loud, was simple and dangerous: this clock had become more than a piece on a mantel. If someone clever—or cruel—had used the train as a timer, a clock could do a very private kind of violence.

At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

1. Open on the locked-room discovery: Ellis arrives at Harben House, meets Inspector Lane and Anna, and is shown the study that is locked from the inside with Lucius Harben dead. Establish stakes, the room's layout (longcase clock, display case, desk), the brass key in the lock, the torn note in the victim's hand and the initial puzzle—no gun on display.
2. Ellis inspects the study in detail: examines the clock (stopped at a specific minute), checks the weapon display (revolver missing or hidden), finds black thread behind the clock and the envelope on the desk. He interviews Iris Harben and Thomas Reed separately—collect their alibis, motives (financial quarrel, threatened sale), and small tells. Inspector Lane warns Ellis about upsetting the investigation but tacitly lets him proceed.
3. Ellis pursues a mechanical hypothesis: the clock's internal train could have been used as a timed trigger. He finds evidence of recent access to the clock's inner case and that the torn note was put in the victim's hand after death. Tensions rise when Ellis confronts Thomas, who admits to servicing the clock recently but denies any role in the death. An unexpected piece of evidence (a fingerprint or a peculiar crease in the envelope flap) points to Iris in a way that seems damning and believable.

There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-003.md>

I went back into the study with Lane's warning folded into the hollow of a sentence I couldn't spend. She'd told me not to touch anything until forensics arrived; I left my hands in my coat and let my eyes do the work. The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. The access panel at the back was a hair ajar; the brass inside looked thumbed, varnish rubbed away where skin or a tool had rested. Fine, fresh scores ringed the latch—hairline marks that flashed when the light caught them, as if a slender implement had been used to lever it.

At the base the black thread hung where I'd seen it: waxed, stiff, snagged on a screw. I followed its line: it looped and ran up toward the movement and vanished behind the plates. That was no stray sewing fibre; laid like that it could be a patient little mechanism, a thing that might nudge a wheel at an appointed minute.

Thomas Reed came in from the workshop, bringing the faint smell of oil with him. He had the thumb-and-forefinger rub that tells you a man is working through a thought. "You were in here recently?" I asked.

He met my gaze. "I was in three days ago to wind it and I stripped the weight-gear to clean the pivots—it's delicate work, Ellis." He paused, then added, "I was out of the shop just before eleven. Ask anyone." The admission sat in the room like a small brass cog: useful, precise, and easily checked.

"You left the panel closed?" I said.

"I always close it when I'm done," he said. He rubbed his thumb as if to work a stubborn splinter free. "I didn't kill him, if that's what you're getting at. I serviced it—winding, cleaning the pivots—but I was gone by then." His voice tightened on the last word.

Lucius's fingers curled around a torn scrap. The ragged edge lay on top of the knuckles; the torn fibres splayed against the skin rather than pressed into it. The blotter beneath showed a neat, round stain—the dark halo of a single shot. The scrap sat on that halo without a smear. If he'd clutched the paper in his last moments the fibres would have been pressed, ink and blood rubbed into the edge. This looked arranged.

"The scrap was put there after the fact," I said, careful to keep my tone even. Accusation is heavy; Lane was watching.

Thomas's face went slack. "Why would someone do that? To make it look—" He stopped.

Forensics arrived just then. They moved with the efficiency of people who practise restraint: a gloved hand to lift, a small vacuum for trace, a careful photograph. The tech at the desk tapped the envelope's diagonal crease with a latexed fingertip. "We lifted a partial print from the flap's crease," he said. "Preliminary lift consistent with Iris Harben."

Iris came in as if the name had called her. She kept her composure; the small motion of smoothing her wedding band was the private thing I'd noticed before. When I asked about the sale and the note she answered with a bluntness that might be armour. "If he sells it, we have nothing left but his arrogance."

For a moment the study felt like a display cabinet for evidence: the stopped hands at eleven-seventeen, the access panel scored with fresh marks, the black thread threading toward the gears, a torn note that read like stagecraft, and an envelope that now carried a lifted print. I kept my hands where Lane could see them and stepped to the clock's case without touching the latch. Forensics had the gloves and the reasons.

What I thought, and was careful not to say out loud, was simple and dangerous: this clock had become more than a piece on a mantel. If someone clever—or cruel—had used the train as a timer, a clock could do a very private kind of violence.

I went back into the study with Lane’s caution still hanging between us. She closed the door behind her and said, in the very words she’d used when I first arrived, “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” The sentence landed like a rule; her eyes supplied everything she didn’t say.

The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

I went back into the study with Lane’s caution still hanging between us. She closed the door behind her and said, in the very words she’d used when I first arrived, “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” The sentence landed like a rule; her eyes supplied everything she didn’t say.

The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

### recent-scene-s-001  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

s-001, 2 scene(s) before this one:

The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No supernatural elements or 'impossible' physics — every action must be explainable by real mechanisms or human trickery.
- The narrator, Ellis, cannot know anything he didn't observe, be told, or reasonably infer; revelations must come by evidence or deduction shown in-scene.

- All significant objects, locations and characters used in scenes must be declared as entities above; later scenes may only refer to these ids.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

I went back into the study with Lane’s caution still hanging between us. She closed the door behind her and said, in the very words she’d used when I first arrived, “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” The sentence landed like a rule; her eyes supplied everything she didn’t say.

The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

### recent-scene-s-001  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

s-001, 2 scene(s) before this one:

The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- All significant objects, locations and characters used in scenes must be declared as entities above; later scenes may only refer to these ids.
- Locked-room constraints are physical: doors and windows can only be manipulated by plausible mechanical means or realistic sleight, and any trick must be demonstrable within the story's scenes.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

I went back into the study with Lane’s caution still hanging between us. She closed the door behind her and said, in the very words she’d used when I first arrived, “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” The sentence landed like a rule; her eyes supplied everything she didn’t say.

The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

### recent-scene-s-001  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

s-001, 2 scene(s) before this one:

The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

I went back into the study with Lane’s caution still hanging between us. She closed the door behind her and said, in the very words she’d used when I first arrived, “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” The sentence landed like a rule; her eyes supplied everything she didn’t say.

The longcase clock took the far wall and held the light. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless. The rear access panel was a hair ajar and the latch sat crooked where it should have been flush. At the base, tucked behind the inner brass and snagged on a small screw, a length of black thread hung, waxed and stiff. A thin line of dust lay above it; below, the wood was cleaner, as if someone had brushed the area in haste.

Opposite the clock the weapons case kept its quiet. One mount was empty; the brass plaque beneath read IVORY REVOLVER. The velvet where a grip had lain was pressed down, an absence that made the rest of the row look oddly whole by comparison.

On Lucius Harben’s desk a sealed envelope sat with a shallow diagonal crease across the flap. When I tilted it the typed line showed through the thin paper, blunt and plain: “DO NOT SELL THE IVORY REVOLVER. THIS IS YOUR LAST WARNING.” I did not open it; forensics would want their say.

Anna Rowe stood in the doorway, practical and steady. She told me she had seen Mr. Harben at breakfast, just after eight, that Mrs. Harben had left for town a little after nine, and that Mr. Reed had called by later and left before eleven. She reminded me she’d been the one to find him at his desk and that he’d still been holding something in his hand when she did.

Iris Harben spoke to me in the small parlour off the foyer. She gave a neat account — she’d been in town that morning to discuss payments connected with the collection — and kept her voice level while she smoothed the edge of her hand against her wedding band. The motion was small and automatic, a private thing trying to steady public calm. She would not be drawn on the envelope; she said only that talk of sales had made her anxious for the house’s finances.

Thomas Reed was in the service room, his hands carrying the faint grains of his work. He said he’d been in the workshop across the square until just before eleven and that a neighbour could confirm it. He spoke quickly, with an impatience that shortened his answers, and kept rubbing the pad of his thumb and forefinger together in that restless way of men who handle small gears. When I asked about the disputed sale he gave a clipped account and shut the subject down.

Lane watched from the doorway as I closed matters with Thomas and then returned to the study. She repeated, without irony, the warning she’d given me at the start: “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis.” Her look after the words said I could look and ask questions, but I must not be a clumsy hand. I told her I understood. That would have to be enough for now.

### recent-scene-s-001  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

s-001, 2 scene(s) before this one:

The cab left me on a wet flagstone, the driver already counting the seconds until he could leave. Harben House sat back from the lane under a low sky; rain freckled the leaded windows and made the oak panels look younger than they were. Inspector Lane stood in the small foyer with her collar up, a constable behind her, the hall already marked off with a strip of tape that had more dignity than utility. “Don’t touch anything until forensics are here, Ellis,” she said when she saw me. Her voice was polite; her eyes were not.

Anna Rowe met me at the study door. She had been the one to find him. “I found him at his desk, Mr. Fletcher. He still had something in his hand,” she told me before she could stop herself. Her hands were steady but her knuckles were white where she gripped a shawl.

The study door was shut. A heavy brass key sat in its lock, the metal dulled by years of handling and scored along one edge. Lane pointed at it without looking: “Locked from the inside,” she said. She did not ask me whether I wanted to see; that would have been an invitation I would have taken if she had given it.

The room beyond smelled of oil and paper and a faint, sharp tang of metal. It was smaller than my head had made it; bookcases leaned in as if gossiping. The longcase clock took up the far wall, an upright thing of walnut and gilt that pulled the light toward it. Its hands were frozen at eleven seventeen; the pendulum hung motionless, a dark tongue. Whatever had stopped it had stopped it cleanly—the access panel at the rear of the case was a hair ajar, a sliver of inner brass visible where the latch sat crooked.

Opposite the clock, a glass-fronted case displayed a row of mounts on velvet. One mount was empty. A little brass label under the gap read IVORY REVOLVER in neat type; the mounting beneath it showed the ghost of a shape, the crushed velvet where the grip had rested. The case held everything else in its place, all the gilded mouths and ivory handles lined up, and then that absence like a missing tooth.

Lucius Harben sat at his desk with his shoulders folded forward as if in sleep. The back of his head caught the light; his fingers curled over a torn scrap. I stepped closer the way you do when you mean to offend nothing, and Lane let me. His chest was still. A neat, round mark on the wood, the kind a single shot makes, stained the blotter beside his hand.

In his palm was a torn note, no larger than my thumb. The fragment I could see read, simply, do not wind. I read the words twice, because a sentence like that felt like a trap or an instruction and I prefer to be polite in the face of either.

At the base of the clock, tangled in the carved scrollwork, a black thread hung, waxed and stiff. It caught my nail when I checked it; it looked absurdly ordinary to be part of anything clever, and for that reason I did not dismiss it.

The windows were latched and the glass unbroken. No sign of forced entry showed on the doorframe; the brass key remained in the lock on the study side. Anna hovered near the threshold, glancing from the body to the clock as if she were still trying to reconcile two different days. Lane watched the room the way a surgeon watches an exposed artery.

I said nothing at first. There was a set of small, precise things here: a stopped clock, a brass key in the lock, an empty space where an ivory revolver should have been, a torn note clutched in a dead man’s hand. The facts were polite and stubborn; they would have to be asked their questions in order. For now there was only the noise of the rain, the smell of oil, and the way the house seemed to be holding its breath.

She had told me not to touch anything until forensics arrived; I kept my hands in my coat and let my eyes do the work. The longcase clock took the far wall and swallowed the light. The access panel at the back was a hair ajar; when I peered in the brass looked thumbed and raw where varnish had been rubbed away. There were fine, fresh scores around the latch—hairline marks that caught the light as if someone had used a slender tool to lever it open.

At the base the black thread hung where I'd seen it: waxed, stiff, caught on a small screw. This time I followed its line with my gaze. It wasn't a loose scrap that had wandered into the case; the thread looped and ran up toward the movement, vanishing behind the plates. If you wanted a thing to move at a chosen minute, a thread laid like that would be the sort of modest, patient device you'd use.

I didn't say any of that aloud. I turned instead to Thomas Reed when he came in from the workshop, his hands smelling faintly of oil. He had that thumb-and-forefinger rub that men in his trade do when they steady themselves. "You were in here recently?" I asked.

He met my eyes and his mouth went flat. He said, "I was in three days ago to wind it and I stripped the weight-gear to clean the pivots—it's delicate work, Ellis." The sentence landed without flourish; it was an admission and a small, professional apology all at once.

"You left the panel ajar?" I asked.

He looked past me at the frame of the clock. "No," he said. "I always close it. I wouldn't leave the case open. I closed it when I left." He rubbed his thumb harder, like a man trying to work a stubborn tooth loose. "I didn't kill him, if that's what you're getting at. I serviced it—winding, cleaning the pivots—but I was out of the shop by ten. Ask anyone." His voice tightened on the last clause.

There was a thing in the dead man's hand that didn't fit with Thomas's timeline. Lucius's fingers were curled around a torn scrap; the ragged edge lay on top of the knuckles, the torn fibres splayed against his skin rather than pressed into it. The blotter beneath showed the neat ring of a round stain, the dark halo that told you where blood had soaked through. The scrap, though, sat on that halo without a smear. If he'd clutched the paper in his last moments it would have been different—the fibres would have been pressed, ink and blood mingled into the edge. This looked staged.

"The scrap's been put there after the fact," I said, and I kept my tone light because accusation is heavy and Lane was watching. "Its fibres lie on top of his fingers. It hasn't been pressed into the skin, and there's no transfer where you'd expect it."

Thomas's cheeks hollowed. "Why would someone do that?" he asked. "To make it look—" He didn't finish.

That was when Lane walked over with the constable and a man from forensics, although they were careful and quick and didn't disturb anything more than a single gloved hand to lift a sample. The forensics man paused at the desk and tapped his latexed finger at the envelope's diagonal crease. "We lifted a partial print from the flap's crease," he told me without flourish. "Preliminary lift consistent with Iris Harben."

Iris appeared then, as if the naming had summoned her. She was composed; the movement of her hand to her wedding band was the small private motion I had seen before. When I asked her about the sale and the note she said, with a bluntness that might have been armour, "If he sells it, we have nothing left but his arrogance."

Her words settled over the room like another clock tuning itself. For a moment everything in the study felt arranged to be observed: the stopped hands at eleven-seventeen, the access panel that shouldn't have been raw with tool-marks, the thread running toward the gears, a torn note that read like stagecraft, and an envelope that now carried a print.

I kept my hands where Lane could see them and stepped to the clock's case. I did not touch the latch; forensics had the gloves and the reason. But the thing I was thinking was plain and dangerous: this wasn't just a prized object anymore. If someone's clever—or cruel—hand had used the train as a timer, the clock could be the mechanism that killed Lucius."}}],"api":"openai-completions","provider":"yuanshi-sg","model":"gpt-5-mini","usage":{"input":6369,"output":4032,"cacheRead":6528,"cacheWrite":0,"reasoning":3008,"totalTokens":16929,"cost":{"input":0,"output":0,"cacheRead":0,"cacheWrite":0,"total":0}},"stopReason":"toolUse","timestamp":1785173266488,"responseId":"chatcmpl-E6JP9tnRRG50uSUGy5K10gG8gSqc5","responseModel":"gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07"}
